# Partnerships, Hiring, and Delegation

Distilled from EP's (@eptwts) knowledge base, eptwts.com. These are EP's opinionated operator heuristics, not universal facts.

This skill covers structuring partnerships, hiring and paying people, and designing the business so the owner can step out of daily work. Core thesis: $0 to $10k/month can be done alone; $10k to $100k requires delegation, outsourcing, and automation. Pair around complementary strengths (marketer x developer), pay on performance, lock incentives before delivering value, and restrict your own time to the four productive activities.

## When to use

- Revenue plateau around $10k/month with the owner doing everything.
- Choosing a cofounder or evaluating a partnership offer.
- Hiring developers, designers, editors, creators, or VAs, and deciding what to pay.
- Structuring equity, revshare, affiliate cuts, or referral deals.
- Acquiring clients for a service or agency; cold outreach that isn't working.
- The owner wants passive-for-them income or to build a team.
- Someone asks the user for free help "as a favor".

## Core principles

**The marketer x developer duo is the most profitable two-person partnership online.** Each covers the other's blind spot. If you can't build, sell someone else's software to prove you can distribute, then partner 50/50 with a hungry developer who lacks distribution. Distribution proof is the asset you bring.

**Restructure around strengths instead of fighting weaknesses.** Hate camera? Faceless brand or hire creators. Hate coding? Partner with a dev who hates distribution. Hate sales calls? Partner with a closer. "Discipline" is often a lie told by people who outsource everything they dislike.

**Be the visionary between businessman and technical.** Understand markets, teams, systems, and distribution; be just technical enough to give developers exact logic. Going deeper steals capacity from visionary work when thousands of qualified developers can be hired.

**Hire talent without a personal brand.** Branded providers charge around 4x market worth; a $5,000+ landing page is almost never justified when a skilled unknown builds better for under $500. Source from forums, Discord, and Telegram rather than X. EP cites quotes differing 10x+ for identical builds ($100k vs $8k) and ~$1.7k/month buying very good talent in India or the Philippines.

**When you find a good developer, never let him go and pay him well.** Genuinely good developers are far rarer than assumed; retention is cheaper than replacement.

**Pay on performance, not retainers.** Retainers breed complacency. If someone refuses performance pay, they don't believe in your product or their results, both disqualifying. EP's editor deal: editors keep 100% of ad revenue plus view-milestone bonuses; EP keeps product sales.

**Lock incentives before helping.** 9 out of 10 people you "put on" for free later claim they didn't need your help. Structure equity, revshare, or affiliate cut before delivering value.

**Brokering is underrated.** Millions can be made purely connecting people who want something with people who can fulfil it. EP's AI-adjacent audience generated 10+ service inquiries daily; his plan was to pass leads to a real engineer for referral revenue.

**Teaching publicly beats cold outreach for agency clients.** Cold outreach from an unknown fails on zero credibility. The two working paths: in-person/local connections where credibility transfers, or inbound via publishing the niche-specific work you do.

**Laziness plus ambition is the CEO combination.** Find the path of least resistance and build systems others fulfil. Hard workers hit a ceiling believing they can do everything personally.

**Build a business you can remove yourself from.** Grind at the start: 16-hour days are for testing, validating, and installing systems, never for repeating manual work. EP's former agency runs on his team at ~10 minutes of his time per week, netting ~$8k/month.

**Only four activities are productive.** Improving the product, working on the offer/funnel, creating content/creatives, talking to clients. Learning is "beneficial, not productive" until it feeds one of the four. Twin filter: does this create value for customers or communicate value to prospects?

**Commit to the validated model.** Give a new model 1-2 months of proper effort, then change approach or quit. But model-hopping is among the worst habits; all the models work, the variable is commitment.

## Workflow

### A. Deciding what to delegate

1. **Log a week of the owner's time.** Tag every block as one of: product, offer/funnel, content/creatives, talking to clients, or "other".
2. **Everything in "other" is a delegation or automation candidate.** Decision point: automatable with code → automate; requires judgment or human touch → VA or specialist; owner-only (vision, key relationships) → keep.
3. **Check the profitability trigger.** If the product is already profitable and the owner is avoiding hiring to protect margins, that is a growth killer; hire now.
4. **Systemize before delegating.** Write the process (SOP, Loom) while the owner is still doing it. Delegate only functions the owner has personally validated.
5. **Structure the team.** One trusted personal assistant overseeing everything; each VA assigned to one small compartment so no single person sees enough to replicate the operation.
6. **Kill meetings.** Default to async text and Loom; nearly every "quick call" fits in one paragraph.
7. **Target the operating model.** 100% hands-on during setup (development + distribution), then systems and near-autopilot. Diversify: EP targets at least a quarter of revenue from automated, low-barrier models.

### B. Hiring a specific role

1. **Define the output standard, not the method.** For creatives, never ask whether they use AI; judge only whether the end product meets the bar.
2. **Source off-brand.** Forums, Discord, Telegram, regional freelancer communities. For content talent, gaming content creators: passionate, cheap, DM directly.
3. **Filter.** Trust the first impression: a candidate who can't follow simple application rules will deviate on the job. Ask "Are you the best at what you do?" Run a small paid test task with a simple system to test trainability; expect most to fail.
4. **Pay on performance.** Offer a base tied to output plus milestone bonuses or revenue share. Refusal of performance pay is disqualifying.
5. **Retain the rare good ones.** Pay a proven developer well and keep them.

### C. Structuring a partnership

1. **Confirm complementary blind spots.** Marketer x developer, visionary x builder, operator x closer. Two people with the same skill is not a partnership.
2. **Prove your side first.** If you bring distribution, show it (a channel, a list, affiliate sales). If you bring build, show shipped work.
3. **Lock incentives in writing before any work.** Equity split, revshare, affiliate cut, who owns what, exit terms.
4. **Prefer percentage-of-upside deals over fees** where the user is the leverage: run someone's X presence for a percentage, broker leads for a referral cut, manage creators for a share.
5. **Avoid public beefs** with competitors or ex-partners; feuds hurt both sides.

### D. Getting clients for a service

1. Start with local or in-person connections where credibility transfers.
2. Publish the niche-specific work you do (teach publicly on X); let inbound come.
3. When you do cold outreach: context on why this person specifically, their benefit first, minimal sell.
4. Network counter-cyclically: befriend the sector's influencers when attention has left it.

## Checklists / templates

### Delegation triage

| Task | Productive category (product / offer / content / clients / other) | Automate (code) | Delegate (VA/specialist) | Keep |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Rule: everything automatable with code gets code; everything else gets a VA; only the four productive activities stay with the owner, and even those get delegated once systemized.

### Hiring filter

- [ ] Followed the application instructions exactly.
- [ ] Answered "Are you the best at what you do?" with self-awareness.
- [ ] Sourced outside personal-brand marketplaces (no status premium).
- [ ] Passed a small trainability test.
- [ ] Accepted performance-based pay.
- [ ] End product meets the standard regardless of tools used.

### Incentive lock template (before delivering value)

- What I deliver: ___
- What they deliver: ___
- Upside mechanism: equity ___% / revshare ___% / affiliate cut ___% / referral fee ___
- Trigger and payment timing: ___
- Ownership of assets created: ___
- Exit terms: ___

### Cold outreach message structure

1. Why this specific person (evidence you know their situation).
2. Their benefit, stated first.
3. One-line proof (case study or published work).
4. Minimal ask.

### Soft-skill curriculum checklist (EP: successful operators know ~80% of these)

- [ ] Market research
- [ ] Offer creation
- [ ] Sales psychology
- [ ] Copywriting
- [ ] Distribution
- [ ] Paid ads
- [ ] Funnels
- [ ] Audience building
- [ ] Delegation
- [ ] Content
- [ ] Email marketing
- [ ] Storytelling
- [ ] Pricing psychology
- [ ] Retention
- [ ] Payment processing
- [ ] Upsells
- [ ] SEO
- [ ] Automation

Use it to pick which skills to learn yourself and which to hire.

## Anti-patterns

- Guaranteed monthly retainers for contributors (EP learned this the hard way).
- Helping someone professionally without locking the incentive first.
- Paying the 4x personal-brand premium for a landing page or design.
- Hiring an agency as a buyer when in-house or direct freelancers are cheaper and more efficient.
- Going deeper technically than needed to spec logic for developers.
- Avoiding hiring to protect margins once profitable.
- Calls and meetings by default.
- Business-model hopping before the 1-2 month validation window.
- Public feuds with competitors.

## Dated / volatile notes

- Freelancer sourcing example names Telegram and the forum zelenka.guru, plus Russian/Ukrainian, Indian, and Filipino talent pools at ~$1.7k/month; rates and platforms change.
- "$0-$10k alone, $10k-$100k delegation" and "AI shrinking team sizes" reflect 2025 conditions.
- Editor deal (100% ad revenue + milestone bonuses) is tied to platform ad-revenue programs.

Source: https://www.eptwts.com/business-strategy — EP (@eptwts) knowledge base, Chapter 01: Business Strategy (scraped 2026-09-15). Lessons reproduced verbatim.

## Partnerships and Hiring

**The marketer × developer duo is the most profitable two-person partnership online.**
The coder builds, the marketer makes it reach and convert; each covers the other's blind spot. If you can't build software, sell somebody else's to prove you can distribute, then find a hungry developer who lacks distribution and partner 50/50 - distribution proof is itself an asset you bring. The same shape holds in AI automation: the visionary + builder duo, one who understands the game and holds the vision, one who brings it to life.

**Restructure around strengths instead of fighting weaknesses.**
Hate camera? Faceless brand or hire creators. Want software but hate coding? Partner with a dev who hates distribution. Want a book but hate writing? Dictate to AI. Hate sales calls? Partner with a closer. "Discipline" is often a lie told by successful people who simply outsource everything they dislike.

**Be the visionary between businessman and technical.**
Understand markets, teams, systems, and distribution, and be just technical enough to give developers exact logic - going deeper is a net negative that steals capacity from visionary work, when thousands of qualified developers can be hired for the rest.

**When you find a good developer, never let him go and pay him well**
- genuinely good developers are far rarer than assumed, and retaining scarce proven talent is cheaper than replacing it.

**Hire talent without a personal brand.**
Providers with followings charge a premium for status - the best-branded charge around 4x market worth, and a $5,000+ landing page is almost never justified when a skilled unknown builds better for under $500. Source from forums, Discord, and Telegram rather than X. Specific arbitrage: Russian and Ukrainian freelancers are often excellent at development and design (found on Telegram and forums like zelenka.guru); quotes for identical projects can differ 10x+ with no quality difference - real example: $100k vs $8k for the same build. Around $1.7k/month buys very good talent in India or the Philippines (~6x local average wage), so expect quality at that price.

**Gaming content creators are the best cheap content-talent pool.**
Most earn nothing, are genuinely passionate, and can be hired inexpensively - DM directly and run a simple system to test trainability; most fail the filter but the hit rate beats other pools. Founders should outsource video content to hungry creators rather than record it themselves.

**Pay on performance, not retainers.**
Retainers breed complacency (I learned this giving guaranteed monthly retainers because I could). If someone refuses performance pay, they either don't believe in your product, don't believe in their results, or both - all disqualifying. The hungry newcomer with something to prove outworks the big agency extracting fees. My editor deal: editors keep 100% of ad revenue plus view-milestone bonuses; I keep product sales.

**Hiring filters:**
trust the first impression - a candidate who can't follow simple rules at the application stage will deviate on the job. "Are you the best at what you do?" instantly reveals whether someone understands their own specialty, their self-perception, and how they rate their skills - most people can't answer at all. When hiring creatives, never ask whether they use AI; judge only whether the end product meets the standard - copy that reads like AI or a site that looks vibe-coded is itself the disqualifying skill issue.

**Never help someone professionally without locking in the incentive first.**
9 out of 10 people you "put on" for free will later claim they didn't need your help. Structure the upside (equity, revshare, affiliate cut) before delivering value, not after.

**Brokering is underrated:**
you can make millions purely connecting people who want something with people who can fulfill it - no product of your own; the skill is sourcing both sides and taking a cut. Concrete case: without ever offering automation services, my AI-adjacent audience generated 10+ service inquiries daily - my plan was to partner with a genuine engineer and pass leads through hands-off for referral revenue.

**Cold outreach basics:**
a pitch with no context, too much sell, and nothing in it for the recipient fails - show why you're messaging this person specifically and lead with their benefit. As an unknown selling automation/AI services, cold outreach mostly fails on zero credibility anyway; the two working paths are in-person/local connections (an uncle's or family friend's business, where credibility transfers) or inbound via publishing the niche-specific automations you build.

**Teaching publicly is the best agency client-acquisition strategy.**
Build an X account teaching people how to do what you do; demonstrating expertise builds authority and clients come inbound with barely any advertising - provided you're actually good at the craft.

**Network counter-cyclically:**
when crypto content disappears from your feed (bear market), that's exactly when to befriend crypto influencers for the next bull run. Relationships are cheap when attention has left a sector and expensive once the cycle turns.

**Avoid public beefs with competitors**
- feuds almost always hurt both sides; keep your enemies close.

## Operations, Delegation, and Systems

**$0→$10k/month you can do alone; $10k→$100k requires delegation, outsourcing, and automation.**
Everything automatable with code should be; everything else gets automated with virtual assistants - create systems that work, then automate them. Build the team the moment the product turns profitable: avoiding hiring to protect margins is one of the worst growth killers, and even with AI shrinking team sizes, owners still want to delegate operating the systems.

**Laziness plus ambition is the CEO combination.**
Find the path of least resistance and build systems others fulfill. Hard workers hit a ceiling believing they can do everything personally; every CEO is "inherently a procrastinator" about mundane tasks - the fix is delegation, not discipline.

**Build a business you can remove yourself from.**
A business requiring your daily presence is barely better than a job (my main income source needs about one hour of daily attention because of systems). Grind at the beginning - 16-hour days are for testing, validating, and installing systems, never for repeating manual work - then systematically delegate every function you fall out of love with. Passive income is never truly passive, but it can be passive for you: my former marketing agency runs on my team at ~10 minutes of my time per week, netting ~$8k/month.

**Operating model per project:**
100% hands-on during a setup phase covering both development and distribution, then systems and near-autopilot. I also target at least a quarter of revenue from automated, low-barrier models as diversification, because internet income is volatile.

**If you own a cashflowing business, be an orchestrator.**
Awareness of what AI makes possible matters more than personally building automations - making them yourself is low leverage when thousands can do it better and cheaper. Ideal loop: have the idea, think through how it should work, hand to the team, move to the next decision.

**VA structure:**
one trusted personal assistant overseeing everything (in my case a childhood friend), each VA assigned to one small component. Compartmentalization means no single VA sees enough to replicate the operation.

**Kill meetings.**
Nearly every "quick call" produces a conclusion that fits in one paragraph - default to asynchronous text and Loom videos for almost all business communication.

**Only four activities are productive:**
improving the product, working on the offer/funnel, creating content/creatives, and talking to clients. Everything else - including learning, until it feeds one of the four - is "beneficial, not productive." Twin filter: does this create value for customers, or communicate value to potential customers? If neither, you're wasting time.

**Validation speed and commitment:**
give a new model 1-2 months of proper effort to show results, then change approach or quit - "great things take years" is partly a psyop that keeps people beating dead horses. But business-model hopping is among the worst habits: commitment applies to the model you validated. The plot twist I tell PDF collectors: all the models work; the variable is commitment.

**The soft-skill reality check:**
it's nearly impossible to teach someone who has never operated online how to make money on the internet - success rests on hundreds of soft skills absorbed passively (intuition for what works, what good design is, how the internet economy functions), acquired only through years of actually operating. The complete curriculum, treated as a checklist: market research, offer creation, sales psychology, copywriting, distribution, paid ads, funnels, audience building, delegation, content, email marketing, storytelling, pricing psychology, retention, payment processing, upsells, SEO, automation - nearly every successful operator I know is well-versed in at least 80% of these.

# Platform Growth Playbooks

Distilled from EP's (@eptwts) knowledge base, eptwts.com. Opinionated operator heuristics; the grey-hat material is documented in references and flagged below, but the Workflow teaches only the whitehat, durable versions.

Core thesis: on engagement-ranked platforms (Instagram especially), a mechanical funnel that turns a post's engagement into a DM conversation is the fastest route from attention to sale. EP's own rule is whitehat before blackhat: no bot, purchased-account, or automation experiment until an organic content machine is already selling the product, and even then the multi-account world is an amplifier, not a foundation. The whitehat funnels below are the parts that hold up.

## When to use

- Building an Instagram (or Reels/Shorts/TikTok) funnel for a digital product, community, or template.
- Designing short-form content that maximizes retention and loops.
- Growing a local-audience page (town, city, niche community) for a local or geo-relevant offer.
- Setting up a clipping/repurposing operation for a creator or brand.
- Riding a major public spectacle or trend with content pages.
- The user asks about buying followers/engagement, multi-account stacks, or SMM panels (answer: explain, then steer away).
- Learning resources (Blackhatworld) or brand-voice cloning with AI.

## Core principles

**Instagram weights engagement heavily; a comment CTA converts that into a DM funnel.** EP's four steps: create a digital product (guide, Discord, Notion template); post reels showing it with "comment X and I'll send it"; the comment flood pushes the post; DM the sales page to every commenter. The comment is both the ranking signal and the lead capture.

**Short loops multiply retention.** EP's 7-second reel: show a pain point, overlay a CTA to read the caption for the solution, write a long caption that funnels to the product. While people read, the video loops repeatedly; more loops mean higher retention and more push.

**Local identity earns follow-backs.** EP's town-page play: pages named for small towns, follow the followers of local business pages, residents recognize the town name and follow back, then funnel to the product and scale with VAs. The durable insight is that geographic or community identity is a strong follow trigger; the whitehat version runs real local pages with real hires and real local content.

**Clipping is legitimate top-of-funnel labor.** Repurposing a streamer's or creator's best moments into short-form is how mass distribution (Tate-style) gets built. Do it with permission or as a hired clipping partner; awareness campaigns are not a scam just because they do not convert directly (see `platform-strategy-and-youtube-mechanics`).

**Attention around public spectacles is farmable, but pick the honest version.** EP's example (rival 2024 election pages funneling both fanbases into one Telegram) is fake-persona spectacle-jacking. The transferable principle: publish genuinely on the spectacle from your own account or a transparently branded page and route interest to owned channels.

**Whitehat before blackhat, always.** Bots, purchased accounts, and experiments usually fail and only make sense as an amplifier on proven product-content fit. In expert niches, audiences can tell AI-generated farm content; it only "works" at mass-market scale where no individual account matters.

**Never buy engagement from public marketplaces.** Valuable engagement depends on who follows the engaging account and niche alignment; anyone selling engagement publicly has none worth buying. Engagement groups and bought signals also dilute your relationship-graph signal (see `x-algorithm-optimization`).

**Blackhatworld is worth reading daily; forums and Discords hide cheap skilled labor.** EP's claim: everything needed to learn social media marketing is there. Read it for mechanics and hiring; do not treat every thread as a plan.

**Clone a brand voice from its top posts.** Open a profile in an incognito browser: logged-out X shows only their top tweets. Scrape those and use them as a voice sample. Use it to study what works in a niche or to model your own voice, not to impersonate.

**Extraordinary lives are a content moat.** EP's 2025 pick for a large personal brand was travel vlogging: extraordinary experiences bring extraordinary impressions, and the lifestyle itself is a moat copycats cannot fake.

## Workflow

Choose the sub-playbook that matches the user's situation, then execute it. All versions are whitehat: one real account per person/brand, real content, engagement earned or paid for transparently.

### A. Instagram comment-to-DM funnel

1. **Build a deliverable worth a comment.** A guide, Notion template, Discord community, checklist, or swipe file that solves one specific problem for the target buyer. If it is not genuinely useful, the funnel burns trust.
2. **Script reels that show it.** Demonstrate the deliverable on screen: the result it produces, a page of it, a walkthrough. End with a clear CTA: "comment [WORD] and I'll send it."
3. **Set up delivery.** Decide manual DMs or a compliant DM-automation tool that sends the link when a comment matches. EP notes auto-DM funnels still work when done well; the bad reputation comes from spammers. Either way, the DM should read like a person wrote it.
4. **Reply to every comment.** Replies add engagement and confirm delivery publicly, which increases comment volume.
5. **Route to the sales page in the DM.** Deliver the free asset first, then the offer link. Keep the DM manual-feeling; automation kills the human touch if it reads as automation.
6. **Measure comment-to-DM-to-sale.** If comments are high but sales are zero, the deliverable is attracting the wrong audience; tighten specificity (see `content-principles-and-audience-quality`).

### B. 7-second loop reel

1. Pick one sharp pain point the buyer recognizes instantly.
2. Record or cut a 7-second clip that shows it (not explains it).
3. Overlay text: "solution in the caption."
4. Write a long caption: the actual solution, then the CTA to the product or the comment keyword from Playbook A.
5. Post and check loops/retention in analytics; iterate on the pain-point hook, not the length.

### C. Localized community pages (whitehat)

1. Choose towns/communities where the offer is actually relevant (local service, local events, regional product).
2. Create a page per location with transparent branding (who runs it, what it is for).
3. Post real local content: local businesses, events, news, useful info. Engage with local business accounts and their followers genuinely.
4. Follow-backs come from recognition of the local name; grow to the target follower count.
5. Funnel to the offer with local relevance ("for [town] residents").
6. Scale with real hires (VAs or local contributors) who manage each page under the same transparent ownership.

### D. Clipping partnership

1. Identify creators whose content the target audience already watches.
2. Get permission or a paid arrangement to clip their content; agree on attribution and CTA.
3. Publish clips to X/Shorts/TikTok with the creator's CTA and, where agreed, your own funnel.
4. If building a clipping team: recruit clippers transparently (Discord, forums), pay them, and offer the service to influencers who want mass short-form distribution. The honest angle is "we distribute your content"; skip the "I make X with clipping" bait framing.

### E. Spectacle- or trend-adjacent content

1. When a major spectacle or launch hits, publish genuine takes, explainers, or utility content about it from your real account or a clearly branded page.
2. Route interest into an owned channel (Telegram, email) with a relevant reason to join.
3. Do not run opposing fake-fan pages or impersonate a side you don't hold.

### F. Decision gate for anything grey-hat

If the user proposes bought followers, engagement panels, account farms, proxies, or automation of TikTok/Instagram uploads:
1. Check the gate: is a whitehat organic machine already selling the product? If not, EP's own rule says do not attempt it.
2. Explain the specific failure modes EP reports (detection and zeroing of automated TikTok/IG uploads; bought aged accounts corrupting geo analytics; public-marketplace engagement being worthless).
3. Redirect to the matching whitehat playbook above. Do not provide an operational multi-account setup.

## Checklists / templates

### Comment-funnel launch checklist
- [ ] Deliverable solves one specific problem for the buyer persona.
- [ ] Reel shows the deliverable on screen, not just talks about it.
- [ ] Single comment keyword; CTA in the video and caption.
- [ ] Delivery path tested (manual or compliant tool); DM reads human.
- [ ] Free asset first, offer link second.
- [ ] Every comment replied to.
- [ ] Tracking: comments, DMs sent, link clicks, sales.

### Loop-reel template
- 0-2s: pain point on screen (visual, not narrated).
- 2-7s: continuation of the pain / hint of result; overlay "solution in caption."
- Caption: 3-8 short lines of the actual solution, then CTA.

### Local page setup sheet
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Location | |
| Offer relevance to this location | |
| Page owner disclosed in bio | yes |
| Content sources (local businesses, events, news) | |
| Manager (real hire) | |
| Follower target before funnel | |

### Clipping agreement outline
- Creator, content scope, attribution format, CTA/link ownership, payment terms, platforms, posting cadence.

### Grey-hat notes: don't run these
Documented from EP for completeness; each is ToS-violating, deceptive, or both. They are in `references/source-lessons.md` verbatim and are not part of any workflow here.
- Snapchat giveaway loop with Quick-Add mass-adding and shoutout-gated giveaways in gambling/forex/crypto niches.
- Town pages as fake persona accounts with no disclosed operator, scaled by VAs.
- Fake rival-fanbase spectacle pages (e.g. opposing election pages) farming both sides into one Telegram.
- Clip-army recruitment via "I make X with clipping" bait.
- Multi-account stacks: proxies, phone farms, anti-detect browsers, emulator automation, aged account suppliers, warm-up procedures; ~50 accounts under one IP.
- Buying TikTok followers from an SMM panel to unlock the 1,000-follower link threshold (EP says it did not hurt reach; it is still bought followers).
- AI-generated post farms at mass-market scale.
- Automated browser uploads to TikTok/Instagram (EP: detected and zeroed; a reason not to, on top of ToS).

## Anti-patterns

- Buying engagement from public marketplaces; EP is unambiguous that anyone selling it publicly has none worth buying.
- Attempting blackhat traffic before a whitehat machine sells the product.
- Automating TikTok or Instagram uploads via browser: detected and zeroed.
- Recommending Selenium for social automation; EP flags it as an amateur signal.
- Buying aged accounts; corrupts geo analytics.
- Running AI-generated farm content in expert niches where audiences can tell.
- Comment funnels with a worthless deliverable; the comment spike comes, the trust does not.
- Auto-DMs that read like spam; the technique's bad reputation comes from poor execution.
- Fake persona pages, undisclosed operators, or impersonating a side of a spectacle.
- Using brand-voice cloning to impersonate rather than to study or model.

## Dated / volatile notes

- Late 2024: EP's travel-vlogging pick as the 2025 niche for a large personal brand.
- 2024 election: EP's spectacle-jacking example (Trump/Biden TikTok pages); event-specific.
- TikTok 1,000-follower link-in-bio threshold and SMM-panel note: platform threshold as of writing; EP's "did not hurt reach" is one account's observation.
- YouTube Shorts tolerating automated uploads while TikTok/Instagram detect them: detection behavior changes; treat as time-stamped.
- Logged-out X showing only top tweets: an interface behavior that may change.
- Instagram's heavy engagement weighting behind the comment funnel: platform mechanics as of writing.

## Platform-Specific and Grey-Hat Playbooks

**Instagram engagement-comment funnel:**
1. Create a digital product (guide, Discord community, Notion template).
2. Post reels showing it off with a "comment X and I will send it to you" CTA.
3. The comment flood blows the post up, because Instagram heavily weights engagement.
4. DM the sales page to every commenter.

**Instagram 7-second-reel loop hack.**
Make a 7-second reel showing a pain point, overlay a CTA to read the caption for the solution, and write a long caption funneling to your product. While people read, the short video loops repeatedly - more loops mean higher retention and more algorithmic push.

**Snapchat giveaway loop:**
1. Create a Snapchat account (optionally seed with 10 US adds via Snap Maps for geo-targeting).
2. Add 100-500 people from Quick Add.
3. Post stories in a profitable niche (crypto, gambling, forex).
4. Run giveaways where entry requires a story shoutout - each entrant advertises you to their friends, a viral loop.
5. Funnel viewers to your paid community or offers.

**Localized Instagram town pages:**
1. Create pages for multiple small American towns (e.g. "wealthclub{town}").
2. Follow the followers of local businesses' pages - residents recognize the town name and follow back.
3. After hitting a follower goal, funnel the audience to your product.
4. Scale by hiring virtual assistants to manage the pages.

**Clip-army playbook:**
1. Repost streamer clips to X.
2. Funnel viewers to a clipping Discord with the angle "I make X with clipping, here's how you can too."
3. Build an army of clippers.
4. Rent the clippers to influencers who want Tate-style mass short-form distribution.

**Spectacle-jacking.**
Build content pages around every major public spectacle and funnel the attention to your offers - e.g. for the 2024 election, a Trump TikTok page and a Biden TikTok page running "who has more supporters / race to 100k" content that farms both fanbases into a public Telegram channel.

**Whitehat before blackhat.**
Do not attempt blackhat traffic generation until a whitehat organic content machine is already selling your product - bots, purchased accounts, and experiments usually fail and only make sense as an amplifier on proven product-content fit.
When you do go serious, multi-account operations require a real stack: proxies, phone farms, anti-detect browsers, browser and emulator automation, aged account suppliers, warm-up procedures, and VAs.
Hard-won specifics: never automate TikTok or Instagram uploads via browser (detected, zeroed; YouTube Shorts tolerates it), Selenium recommendations signal an amateur, buying aged accounts corrupts your geo analytics, and I have run ~50 accounts under one IP - multi-accounting is a grey area that mostly goes unpunished.
At mass-market scale, AI-generated posts and account farms demonstrably work (bans are irrelevant when no individual account matters) - but not in expert niches where audiences can tell.
Buying TikTok followers from an SMM panel just to unlock the 1,000-follower link-in-bio threshold did not hurt my reach, since follower count is not a ranking factor.
But never buy engagement from public marketplaces: valuable engagement depends on who follows the engaging account and niche alignment - anyone selling engagement publicly has none worth buying.

**Blackhatworld is the one forum worth reading daily.**
Everything you need to learn social media marketing is there; forums and Discords are also where cheap skilled labor hides.

**Misc tools and picks.**
To clone a brand voice with AI, open a profile in an incognito browser - logged-out X shows only their top tweets - and have Grok write a quick scraping script.
My 2025 niche pick for a large personal brand: travel vlogging - extraordinary lives bring extraordinary impressions, and the lifestyle itself is the content moat (as of late 2024).

# Platform Strategy and YouTube Mechanics

Distilled from EP's (@eptwts) knowledge base, eptwts.com. Opinionated operator heuristics.

Core thesis: platforms differ sharply in traffic quality and durability. X has the highest-quality, lowest-volume traffic and is the easiest place to build a following; YouTube long-form is the most durable asset and out-earns short-form by orders of magnitude for anything targeted; short-form is top-of-funnel only. Use every platform purely for discovery and convert in owned channels (email, Telegram), because platforms can delete your access to your audience with one click.

## When to use

- Deciding where to spend content effort for a given offer (B2B service, software, info product, community).
- Launching a YouTube channel or diagnosing why videos are not being pushed.
- Deciding how to pitch inside content without tanking retention.
- Planning cross-platform repurposing (X to Instagram, English to other languages).
- Building the owned-audience layer (email/Telegram) and using it to seed platform virality.
- Choosing faceless vs on-camera distribution, or which existing community to align with.

## Core principles

**The traffic-quality map decides the mix.** EP: TikTok and Instagram are low-quality, high-volume; YouTube high-quality, medium-volume; X highest-quality, lowest-volume. X and YouTube long-form have the highest view-to-sale ratios, partly because both let you take users off-platform without friction. For organic B2B, hyperfocus on those two; they are sufficient alone.

**Grow on X first, then propagate.** X is the easiest large platform to build a following on, sets trends others copy, and a base there propels virality elsewhere (the Tate playbook). It is also the most stable: rarely bans, strikes, shadowbans, or sudden algorithm shifts. Bonus mechanic: a timeline of hundreds of small value posts is one extensive sales letter, which is why X creators can command more trust than YouTubers.

**YouTube is the most durable content platform; not posting there while selling something targeted is watching money burn.** Videos earn for a year or more: one summer-2023 video still averaged ~$70/day in sales a year later; another product averaged $200/day at 95% profit from one video per week. For software, one YouTube view is worth roughly 50 reel views; one of EP's brands has 140k YouTube subs vs 50k Instagram followers with YouTube revenue on the order of 100x higher. Only Google-ranked articles match the evergreen snowball.

**Short-form is top-of-funnel, not a converter.** Use TikTok/Reels/Shorts for a first impression at scale, then route viewers to email, YouTube, and podcasts where trust is built. Fresh-account virality is achievable fast with a good niche and format (EP: 10-minute TikTok edit, fresh account, 120k views in 8 hours, leads to email). Expecting cold short-form traffic to convert directly is a skill issue.

**Translation and cross-platform arbitrage are underused.** Proven English viral formats are rarely tested in other languages; translating money-Twitter content into French goes viral in underserved markets. Repurposing X posts to Instagram is one of the fastest brand plays because X concentrates the best thinkers while far fewer normies use it. Post natively wherever a platform is boosting media (X's video push gave ~10x).

**Hunt temporary platform quirks; run cheap tests over assumptions.** Example: the window when YouTube polls got 50k+ views and allowed links. Loopholes never last, but a solid organic base plus short-term exploits compounds. Algorithms change often; test (EP's Instagram experiment: seed 500-1,000 followers before the first reel to shape audience targeting).

**A fresh YouTube channel's first 6-10 videos are a test, not a warm-up.** YouTube evaluates CTR, retention, watch time, and session watch time on that free impression burst and stops feeding impressions if metrics are weak. If none get pushed, the videos are not good enough.

**Search traffic out-converts recommendations ~4x, and search is easier to manipulate.** Someone searching has explicit intent; EP makes 4x more from YouTube search than browse. Research high-intent keywords (vidIQ), put the keyword in the title, build presence on niche forums where buyers gather. Related play: watch X for emerging AI trends and publish YouTube videos before search supply catches up.

**Never link YouTube videos from other platforms expecting reach.** Each discovery source (external, search, browse) is a separate ecosystem with its own metrics; off-platform clicks bring low-intent viewers whose poor retention hurts the video. Diagnose with data: find where views came from, then check CTR and average view duration among browse/recommended viewers specifically.

**The permanent-VSL structure keeps pitching out of your content.** Pitching directly in social content suppresses reach because viewers click away when the plug starts. Instead, make one long video that is your standing sales letter and end every regular video by redirecting to it. For Shorts (no comment links), attach a long-form video (the VSL or a 30-second bridge with a CTA title) via the related-video feature and put the link in that video's description; the button is visible without opening comments.

**Watch time and retention are the metric YouTube actually weights.** EP's grey-hat observation: a 1-minute video at 0.25x registers as 4 minutes (400% retention), which viewer farms exploit. Don't run it; do design for retention.

**Own the relationship, rent the discovery.** Every platform is the top of a funnel: X to Telegram to product; Shorts to long-form to newsletter to product. A ban should never touch your email or Telegram list; if the account dies, owned channels let you respawn within days. An owned audience also makes virality partially self-serve: send daily value, then push that audience at each new post so the early engagement spike triggers wider distribution.

**Faceless funnels work; align with an existing community before building your own lane.** Faceless content into Telegram plus newsletter pulls people in without a camera; once resourced, hire creators. Every mainstream influencer traces to an origin community (Tate from money Twitter, Adin Ross from NBA 2K, Logan Paul from Vine, Nelk from pranks). Creating your own lane from day one is how you stay invisible.

## Workflow

### Part A: pick the platform mix for an offer

1. **Classify the offer.** B2B service or high-ticket; software; info product or community; mass-market low-ticket. Ask what the user sells and who buys.

2. **Map to the traffic-quality tiers.**
   - B2B / high-ticket / software: X + YouTube long-form only. Skip short-form until those are running; per EP they are sufficient alone.
   - Info product or community with a defined niche: X first, YouTube long-form second, short-form as top-of-funnel once there is a place to route viewers (email/Telegram/YouTube).
   - Mass-market low-ticket: short-form for first impressions at volume, but still route into owned channels; do not expect direct conversion.

3. **Sequence: X first.** Unless the user already has a base elsewhere, start on X (easiest to grow, most stable, builds the sales-letter timeline). See `x-growth-from-zero`. Once X has a base, propagate: repurpose proven X posts to Instagram, translate top performers into an underserved language if the user has that market access.

4. **Build the owned layer before scaling discovery.** Set up email and/or Telegram, commit to daily useful sends, and add the call-to-action into every platform's bio/pinned/description. Rule: a platform ban should never touch the list.

5. **Decide faceless vs on-camera.** If the user will not be on camera, run faceless: text on X, faceless YouTube/Shorts into Telegram and newsletter, hire creators later. Either works if the product is good.

6. **Pick the origin community.** Identify the existing community the user genuinely belongs to and connect the content to it before branching out.

7. **Schedule cheap quirk tests.** Reserve a small slice of effort for testing current platform boosts (native video during a media push, new formats). Log results; drop what stops working.

### Part B: YouTube channel launch procedure

1. **Keyword research before recording.** Use vidIQ (or equivalent) to find high-intent search keywords relevant to the product. Prioritize search-driven topics for the first batch; search converts ~4x browse and is easier to rank.

2. **Trend-front-running (optional).** Monitor X for emerging trends in the niche; script videos on them before YouTube search supply catches up.

3. **Record the permanent VSL first.** One long video that is the standing sales letter for the offer. This is the only place the pitch lives.

4. **Produce the first 6-10 videos as a quality test.** Keyword in the title; design for CTR (title/thumbnail), retention, and session watch time. End every video by redirecting to the VSL rather than pitching inline.

5. **Do not drive external traffic to them.** No mass-linking from X, email, or Discord expecting a push; external low-intent clicks hurt retention metrics. External links are fine only as a subscriber-building side effect.

6. **Evaluate the burst.** If at least some of the first 6-10 videos are pushed: keep the format, scale weekly. If none: the videos are not good enough. Do not blame the algorithm; fix hook, retention, and topic-intent match, then run another batch.

7. **Diagnose any underperformer with data, not advice.** Open analytics: where did views come from? Then check CTR and average view duration among browse/recommended viewers specifically. Anything else is speculation.

8. **Add Shorts as top-of-funnel.** Attach the VSL (or a 30-second bridge video with a CTA title) via the related-video feature; put the link in that video's description. Route Shorts viewers to long-form, then to the newsletter.

9. **Compound.** Publish weekly; EP's evidence is that single videos keep selling a year later. Push each new upload to the owned list to seed early engagement.

## Checklists / templates

### Platform selection matrix (EP's map)
| Platform | Traffic quality | Volume | Off-platform friction | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X | Highest | Lowest | Low | Grow first; trust via timeline; network |
| YouTube long-form | High | Medium | Low | Durable converter; search intent |
| YouTube Shorts / TikTok / Reels | Low | High | High | Top-of-funnel first impressions only |
| Email / Telegram | Owned | n/a | n/a | Conversion; ban insurance; virality seeding |

### YouTube pre-launch checklist
- [ ] 6-10 video topics chosen from high-intent search keywords (vidIQ).
- [ ] Keyword in every title.
- [ ] Permanent VSL recorded; every video ends by redirecting to it.
- [ ] No inline pitches inside regular videos.
- [ ] No external-traffic campaign planned for launch.
- [ ] Owned channel (email/Telegram) CTA in descriptions.
- [ ] Shorts plan: related-video attached to VSL or bridge video.

### Underperformance diagnosis script
1. Pull traffic sources for the video.
2. Isolate browse/recommended viewers.
3. Read CTR and average view duration for that segment only.
4. Low CTR: title/thumbnail. Low AVD: hook/pacing/topic mismatch. Both fine but no impressions: the channel failed the initial test; improve the next batch.

### Funnel templates
- X post -> Telegram/email -> product.
- Short -> long-form video -> newsletter -> product.
- Faceless short-form -> Telegram channel + newsletter -> product (hire creators once resourced).

## Anti-patterns

- Building on TikTok/Instagram alone for a B2B or software offer; the traffic is low-quality and hard to move off-platform.
- Expecting short-form to convert directly; awareness precedes conversion.
- Linking YouTube videos from other platforms and expecting algorithmic reach; it pollutes retention.
- Pitching inside content; viewers click away and retention tanks. Use the permanent VSL.
- Treating the first 6-10 videos as a warm-up; they are the test.
- Diagnosing YouTube with generic advice instead of source-segmented CTR and AVD.
- Relying on ad revenue; advertisers pay more for the first 5 seconds than you earn from the video.
- Keeping the whole audience on one platform; bans arrive in waves.
- Creating your own lane from day one instead of aligning with an existing community.
- Playback-speed or viewer-farm retention manipulation; EP flags it as grey-hat. Don't run it.

## Dated / volatile notes

- X video push: media got ~10x boost; EP's ad benchmark from that period was $138 for 5M impressions on X ads (period-specific).
- YouTube polls window: 50k+ views with external links allowed; a closed loophole cited as the archetype of a temporary quirk.
- Summer-2023 video still ~$70/day a year later; $200/day at 95% profit from one video/week; 140k YouTube vs 50k IG with ~100x revenue: EP's specific brands, 2023-2025.
- Search 4x browse and 1 YouTube view ~ 50 reel views (for software) are EP's measured ratios, not platform constants.
- vidIQ is the named keyword tool at time of writing.
- Instagram follower-seeding experiment (500-1,000 followers before the first reel) is an untested-at-scale hypothesis EP ran as a cheap test.

## Platform Strategy

**The traffic-quality map.**
TikTok and Instagram: low-quality, high-volume. YouTube: high-quality, medium-volume. Twitter/X: highest-quality, lowest-volume.
X and YouTube long-form have the highest view-to-sale ratios, partly because both let you take users off-platform without friction.
For organic B2B marketing, hyperfocus on just those two - they are sufficient on their own.

**Grow on X first, then propagate.**
X is the easiest large platform to build a following on, sets trends the others copy later, and a base there propels virality everywhere else - the Tate playbook.
It is also the most stable platform: unlike TikTok/YouTube/Instagram you rarely face bans, strikes, shadowbans, or sudden algorithm shifts, so the audience asset is more durable.
A bonus mechanic: your accumulated timeline of hundreds of small value posts is one extensive sales letter, building more trust than periodic long-form videos - which is why X creators can command more trust than YouTubers.

**YouTube is the most durable content platform.**
Videos keep earning for a year or more: one summer-2023 video still averaged ~$70/day in sales a year later; another product averaged $200/day at 95% profit from one video per week.
For software, one YouTube view is worth roughly 50 reel views - 10 minutes of one person's attention beats 15 seconds of fifty people's; one of my brands has 140k YouTube subscribers vs 50k Instagram followers with YouTube revenue on the order of 100x higher.
Anyone selling something targeted who is not posting on YouTube is watching money burn. The evergreen snowball is matched only by Google-ranked articles.

**Short-form is top-of-funnel, not a converter.**
Use TikTok/Reels/Shorts to give millions a first impression, then route viewers into email lists, YouTube, and podcasts where trust and buying intent are built.
Short-form virality on a brand-new account is still achievable fast with a good niche and format - no warm-up needed: I edited a TikTok in 10 minutes, posted on a fresh account, and hit 120k views in 8 hours, with the leads routed straight to an email list.
Awareness content and clipping campaigns are not a scam just because they don't directly convert - awareness precedes conversion, and expecting cold short-form traffic to convert directly is a skill issue.

**Translation and cross-platform arbitrage.**
Proven English viral formats have rarely been tested elsewhere: translating viral tweets or money-Twitter content into languages like French goes viral in those underserved markets.
Similarly, repurposing X posts to Instagram is one of the fastest brand plays - X concentrates the best thinkers while far fewer normies use it, so proven X content can ride from 0 to 100k IG followers.
And post videos natively wherever a platform is boosting media: during X's video push, media got roughly a 10x boost, and my ad benchmark from the period was $138 for 5M impressions on X ads.

**Hunt temporary platform quirks and exploit them hard while they last.**
Example: the period when YouTube polls reliably got 50k+ views and allowed links driving traffic anywhere.
Loopholes are never sustainable, but a solid organic/paid base plus short-term exploits compounds fast.
Algorithms change often - cheap tests beat assumptions (e.g., my Instagram experiment seeding 500-1,000 followers before the first reel, on the theory that follower interests and geolocation seed the algorithm's audience targeting).

## YouTube Mechanics

**A fresh channel's first 6-10 videos get a free impression burst - treat it as the quality bar.**
YouTube evaluates click-through rate, retention, watch time, and session watch time on that burst and stops feeding impressions if metrics are weak.
If none get pushed, the videos are not good enough - it is a test, not a warm-up.

**Search traffic out-converts recommendations ~4x.**
Someone searching "how to lose weight" has explicit intent; I make 4x more from YouTube search than browse - and search algorithms are much easier to manipulate than recommendation algorithms.
Research high-intent keywords relevant to your product with vidIQ and put the keyword in the title; build presence on niche forums where buyers gather.
A related play: monitor X for emerging AI trends and publish YouTube videos on them before search supply catches up - X surfaces trends days before mainstream demand hits YouTube search.

**Never link your YouTube videos from other platforms expecting reach.**
YouTube treats each discovery source - external links, search, browse/home - as a separate ecosystem with separate engagement metrics; off-platform clicks bring low-intent viewers whose poor retention hurts the video, and external traffic does not trigger algorithmic push.
It helps only indirectly: external viewers who subscribe or engage later see your videos in their feeds.
To diagnose underperformance, get data before advice: find where views actually came from, then check CTR and average view duration specifically among browse/recommended viewers - anything else is speculation.

**The permanent-VSL structure keeps pitching out of your content.**
Make one long video that acts as your standing sales letter and end every regular video by redirecting to it - this preserves the retention metrics of normal content while funneling every viewer to the sales asset.
Extension for Shorts, which don't allow comment links: attach a long-form video (the VSL, or even a 30-second bridge video with a CTA title) via the "related video" feature and put the link in that video's description - it converts better than comment links because the button is visible without opening comments.

**Watch-time quirk: playback speed multiplies retention.**
A 1-minute video watched at 0.25x registers as 4 minutes of watch time - 400% retention - which viewer farms exploit.
Grey-hat, but it reveals that watch time/retention is the metric YouTube actually weights.

## Own the Relationship, Rent the Discovery

**Use platforms purely for discovery; convert in owned channels.**
Every platform is the top of a funnel: X to Telegram to product; Shorts to long-form to newsletter to product.
Pitching directly in social content suppresses reach - viewers click away when the plug starts, tanking retention and future distribution.
And platforms can delete your access to your audience with one click (large YouTube channels get banned in waves): a ban should never touch your email or Telegram list - if your account dies, owned channels let you respawn within days.

**An owned audience makes virality partially self-serve.**
Move followers onto an email list or Telegram, send useful content daily to keep them engaged, then push that audience at each new post - the early engagement spike triggers the platform algorithm to distribute it wider, on any platform.

**Faceless funnels work.**
Faceless content pushing traffic into a Telegram channel and newsletter pulls people into your ecosystem without being on camera; once resourced, hire creators and diversify distribution rather than making videos yourself.
Auto-DM funnels also still work for growth when done well - I used one on my own account; the technique's bad reputation comes from spammers executing it poorly.

**Align with an existing community before building your own lane.**
Every mainstream influencer traces to one origin community: Tate from money Twitter, Adin Ross from NBA 2K, Logan Paul from Vine, Nelk from pranks.
Connect your personality to a community people already care about, then branch out - creating your own lane from day one is how you stay invisible.

# Prompting Techniques

Distilled from EP's (@eptwts) knowledge base, eptwts.com. These are EP's opinionated operator heuristics, not universal facts.

This skill helps you convert a messy request into a precise instruction set and apply the handful of prompting patterns EP considers worth knowing. Core thesis: clear instructions beat raw model intelligence. The more room you leave a model to infer intent, the further the output drifts; a person of average ability with precise step-by-step instructions outperforms a genius with messy ones.

## When to use

- The user's prompt is a single broad question and the answer came back generic.
- The user wants a reusable prompt or system prompt for a recurring task.
- The user needs sharper, more specific advice than a plain question yields (role assignment).
- The user faces a contested question where opposing experts disagree (multi-role debate).
- A chat is performing exceptionally well and the user wants to keep that behavior.
- An AI builder or weaker tool keeps misinterpreting the user's instructions.
- The user asks what prompt-engineering fundamentals to learn.

## Core principles

**Every good prompt has five parts.** Role assignment; context (or a context-collection process such as an interview); step-by-step instructions; an example output structure; rules. Prompts do not need to be long, but the more conditions you set, the more curated the output, no matter how smart models get.

**Clear instructions beat raw intelligence.** Broad prompts will never match the output you imagined. Reduce inference room: state topic, audience, format, success criteria.

**Role assignment steers which training data gets accessed.** EP's example: plainly asking for a CPA marketing method returned generic results; "you are a BlackHatWorld moderator" returned specific ones. Even "take a high IQ, rational, first-principles approach" noticeably sharpens advice. Caveat: role bias does not qualify data quality; a model hooked to a specialized knowledge base beats its general state.

**Multi-role debate is the overlooked upgrade to role assignment.** Assign two or more expert roles to the same problem, make them debate, output the refined synthesis. Council-of-experts truth filter: simulate polar opposites (carnivore vs. vegan) and ask for common ground; conclusions opposing camps share hold the most truth.

**Have the AI write and improve its own instructions (recursive prompting).** Ask LLM #1 "what is the best way to prompt {X idea} so it gives {Y output}", send the result to LLM #2, inspect, ask it to edit the prompt, store the polished version in a prompt library.

**Serialize a great session.** When a chat is performing exceptionally well: "your current state is perfect - send me a prompt in markdown that I can send to another LLM so it acts as a clone of you." Reuse as a system prompt anywhere.

**Keep a prompt-engineer rewriter as a standing system prompt.** It converts messy questions into precise instructions: assign expert role, state topic simply, break into parts, demand examples/steps, specify output format, name the audience, define success.

**Context collection beats rules.** The secret behind viral mega-prompts is the interview at the start, not the rules; have the model gather context question by question before producing anything.

**Translator pattern for weaker tools.** When an AI builder misunderstands, give a stronger model (Claude) a screenshot plus your idea and have it write unambiguous instructions for the builder: a prompt writing a better prompt.

**Learn the fundamentals and prompt intuitively.** Meta-prompting, chain-of-thought, few-shot, self-refining prompts, prompt-chaining, role-based prompting, socratic prompting, plus how an LLM processes a query.

## Workflow

1. **Capture the raw request.** Take the user's messy question as-is. Identify what is missing among: role, topic, audience, constraints (budget, time, tools), desired output format, definition of success.
2. **Decide whether to interview first.** If the task depends on the user's situation (business, audience, goals), add a context-collection window: the prompt must instruct the model to ask one question at a time before producing anything. If stored profiles exist, inject them instead (see `context-engineering-profiles`).
3. **Assign the role.** Pick the most specific persona whose training data you want (a niche forum moderator, a direct-response copywriter, a first-principles rationalist). For contested topics, assign two opposing experts and require a debate plus synthesis.
4. **Write the instruction in the five-part structure.** Role → context/interview → numbered steps → example output structure → rules (constraints, banned behaviors, success definition). Keep it as short as the conditions allow.
5. **Run the rewriter if the user wants speed.** Paste the raw question into the prompt-engineer rewriter template below and use its output.
6. **Iterate recursively.** Send the prompt to a second model, inspect output, ask it to edit the prompt. Store the polished version in the user's prompt library.
7. **If the session is excellent, serialize it.** Ask the model for a markdown clone-prompt and save it as a system prompt.
8. **If the target is a weaker builder tool,** have Claude translate: screenshot + idea → unambiguous instructions for the builder.
9. **Verify output.** Check hallucinations against sources; role assignment does not guarantee data quality.

## Checklists / templates

### Good-prompt checklist

- [ ] Role assigned (specific, not "helpful assistant")
- [ ] Context provided, or an interview step that collects it one question at a time
- [ ] Step-by-step instructions
- [ ] Example output structure
- [ ] Rules: constraints, banned behaviors, audience, definition of success

### Prompt-engineer rewriter (system prompt)

```
You are a prompt engineer. Your only job is to rewrite the user's messy question into a precise instruction for an LLM. Do not answer the question.

For every input:
1. Assign the most specific expert role for the topic.
2. State the topic in one simple sentence.
3. Break the request into its component parts.
4. Demand concrete examples, exact steps, and numbers where relevant.
5. Specify the output format (list, table, steps, word count).
6. Name the audience and their level.
7. Define what a successful answer must contain.
8. Add rules that remove vagueness (budget, timeframe, constraints, what to exclude).

Output only the rewritten prompt, ready to paste.
```

Before/after from the source:

- Before: "How do I market my business?"
- After: "You're a marketing expert. Give me 3 marketing strategies under $1,000 that worked for real businesses and can start this week, with exact steps and common mistakes."

### Multi-role debate template

```
Assign two experts with opposing views on [problem]: [Role A] and [Role B].
Round 1: each states their position and strongest arguments.
Round 2: each rebuts the other.
Round 3: identify every conclusion both agree on.
Output: the shared conclusions first, then a refined synthesis with the remaining disagreements and what evidence would settle them.
```

### Recursive prompting

```
LLM #1: "What is the best way to prompt {X idea} so it gives {Y output}? Write the prompt."
LLM #2: run the generated prompt. Then: "Inspect your output. Edit the prompt so the output would be better on [criteria]. Return the improved prompt."
Store the final version.
```

### Session serialization

```
Your current state is perfect - send me a prompt in markdown that I can send to another LLM so it acts as a clone of you.
```

### Translator pattern

```
[attach screenshot of the builder's current state]
I am using [builder tool]. What I want: [idea in plain words]. It keeps misunderstanding me.
Write unambiguous, step-by-step instructions I can paste into the builder to get exactly this.
```

## Anti-patterns

- Broad one-line questions expecting curated answers.
- Assuming a role makes the data accurate; specialized knowledge injected beats persona alone.
- Writing long rule lists without a context-collection step.
- Running a great prompt once and losing it; keep a prompt library.
- Trusting refusals or compliance blindly. EP notes refusals are often soft and blunt pushback occasionally gets compliance (April 2025); do not use this to push past legitimate safety or policy limits.

## Dated / volatile notes

- Good-prompt checklist, multi-role debate: posted May 2025, practice might be outdated.
- Role assignment examples: August 2025.
- Recursive prompting, rewriter, translator pattern: March 2025.
- Serialize a session: February 2025.
- Fundamentals list and soft refusals: April 2025.

# Selling Without Sales Calls

Distilled from EP's (@eptwts) knowledge base, eptwts.com. These are EP's opinionated operator heuristics, not universal facts.

This skill produces a DM-close script skeleton and a landing page checklist. Core thesis: the public hates sales calls. A visible "buy now" button can outperform a booked-call funnel; nothing under ~$2k should need a call; high-ticket should close in ~10 DMs; and the best cold DM is a plain statement of what you do and exactly how it benefits the recipient. EP earned seven figures without a single sales call or VSL.

## When to use

- The user is designing a checkout or booking flow for an info product, community, or service.
- The user wants to write cold or warm DMs, especially to B2B or sophisticated buyers.
- A prospect asked the price and the user is unsure whether to state it.
- The user's funnel has a long VSL or application-call step in front of a sub-$2k offer.
- The user is spending 30+ minutes per prospect convincing them.
- The user wants the simplest possible setup to start selling.

## Core principles

**A buy-now button beats a booked call for anything under ~$2k.** EP: "as a buyer I won't book a call for anything under ~$2k either." Calls add friction the public resents; he earned seven figures without taking a single sales call or making a VSL.

**When a prospect asks the price, state it. "Let's hop on a call" gets you blocked.** Dodging the number reads as a trap; stating it reads as confidence.

**High-ticket should close in a short DM exchange (~10 messages).** Needing a 30-minute convincing session signals the offer or messaging is weak. The better the product and messaging, the less persuasion is required - if you're hard-convincing, fix the offer, not the script.

**The best cold DM is a plain statement of what you do and how it benefits the recipient.** EP's exact form: "hey, I do XYZ, {how it benefits you}" beats every script. Obvious sales tactics kill B2B deals with sophisticated buyers; part of the job is judging whether the prospect will see through canned techniques.

**State your non-negotiable price up front before explaining scope.** It filters time-wasters expecting the offer at 10% of its worth. It costs some raw conversion but saves enormous back-and-forth.

**Match funnel aggressiveness to traffic temperature.** Warm organic traffic: plain copy and a buy-now button; the emotional persuasion was already done by your content, and a 60-minute unskippable VSL only adds friction. Cold traffic in markets like healthcare or insurance: long VSLs still work.

**Minimum viable stack: landing page + buy-now button + traffic.** Don't overbuild funnels before proving traffic converts on the simplest possible page.

**Faceless works.** EP sold many types of digital products without showing his face, taking a call, or making a VSL - landing page, content-driven traffic, and self-serve checkout replace personal branding.

## Workflow

Gather: the offer, price, whether traffic is warm (your content) or cold (outbound/ads), buyer sophistication (consumer vs operator/B2B).

1. **Route by price.** Under ~$2k: no call, ever. Buy-now button on a landing page; DMs only to answer questions. $2k and up: DM close targeting ~10 messages; offer a call only if the buyer requests one, never as a gate.

2. **Route by traffic temperature.** Warm (they consumed your content): plain copy, proof, buy-now. Cold (outbound/ads in healthcare/insurance-style markets): a long VSL is acceptable; otherwise still prefer plain copy. Do not put a VSL in front of warm traffic.

3. **Build the minimum stack first.** Landing page (EP's baseline: build with bolt.new) + buy-now via Whop (or Gumroad) + traffic. Only add email sequences, upsells, and BNPL after the simple page has produced sales. See `funnels-and-owned-channels` for the capture layer.

4. **Write the DM opener.** Use the plain-statement template below. Strip every recognizable "technique" (fake compliments, loom-video bait, "quick question?"). For sophisticated buyers, assume they've seen every script.

5. **Handle the price ask.** State the number in the next message. Then scope. Never "let's hop on a call" as the answer to "how much?"

6. **Close in ~10 messages.** Use the skeleton below. If you're past 10 and still convincing, note the objection - it's a messaging or offer defect to fix on the page, not a reason to push harder.

7. **Send the buy link, not a calendar link.** For high-ticket, use a checkout link (Whop supports high-ticket checkout links and BNPL). Follow up once; then let the content keep warming them.

8. **Review the landing page against the checklist** and confirm it deviates from the standard info-product template (sameness pattern-matches to scam).

## Checklists / templates

### Cold DM template (EP's exact form)

```
hey, I do XYZ, {how it benefits you}
```

Filled example structure (replace brackets; keep it one plain sentence):

```
hey, I do [what you do, in the words a peer would use], [the specific benefit to this recipient - a number, an outcome, or a removed headache].
```

Rules: no compliment opener, no "quick question", no mystery. State price if they ask, or lead with it for high-ticket.

### Price-first variant (high-ticket, sophisticated buyers)

```
hey, I do [XYZ] for [type of business] - [benefit]. It's $[non-negotiable price]. If that's in range, here's how it works: [2-3 lines of scope].
```

Why lead with price: it filters people expecting the offer at 10% of its worth and saves the back-and-forth.

### ~10-message DM close skeleton

```
1. You:   plain statement (template above)
2. Them:  interest / "what does that involve?" / "how much?"
3. You:   price (if not already stated) + one-line scope
4. Them:  question or objection
5. You:   direct answer + one proof point (a result, not a screenshot wall)
6. Them:  second question / fit check
7. You:   answer; state who it is NOT for (qualification)
8. Them:  "ok how do we start?"
9. You:   checkout link (BNPL option noted for high-ticket) + what happens after payment
10. Them: paid / "let me think"
   You:   if "think": one follow-up later; no pressure sequence.
```

Decision point: if a "call" is requested by the buyer, take it - but never require it. If you're still convincing at message 10, stop and fix the offer/page.

### Landing page checklist (warm traffic, no VSL)

- [ ] Plain copy stating the transformation (see `info-products-sell-transformation`).
- [ ] Price visible; no "apply to learn pricing" for anything under ~$2k.
- [ ] Prominent buy-now button (Whop/Gumroad checkout).
- [ ] BNPL enabled on high-ticket.
- [ ] Layout deviates from the standard info-product template.
- [ ] No unskippable long VSL for warm traffic (allowed only for cold traffic in VSL-tolerant markets).
- [ ] Not called a "course."
- [ ] No promised income figures (see `ethical-selling-and-grifter-detection`).
- [ ] Works without a face or personal brand (self-serve checkout).
- [ ] Instrumented (EP uses PostHog session replays to watch where people drop).

## Anti-patterns

- Gating a sub-$2k offer behind a booked call or application.
- Answering "how much?" with "let's hop on a call."
- Scripted DM openers with recognizable tactics sent to sophisticated buyers.
- 30-minute convincing sessions - a symptom of a weak offer.
- A 60-minute unskippable VSL in front of warm organic traffic.
- Building multi-step funnels before a plain page has converted.
- Hiding the price to "get them on the phone."

## Dated / volatile notes

- Whop high-ticket checkout links and built-in BNPL referenced as of the source (Splitit BNPL benchmark 2025-09).
- bolt.new for landing pages and Whop for payments in EP's minimal online business (2025-03).
- Long VSLs still work on cold traffic in healthcare/insurance - market-specific, may shift.

## Related (from Platform Mechanics & Payment Infrastructure)

Proof of simplicity: I set a friend up with a proven product format plus scripted UGC videos, and sales arrived within two days - execution of a known formula, not novelty. And simple products still work: a PDF (traffic-generation methods plus community access) did $10k in the first 2 hours and ~$35k on day one via an X lead-magnet funnel into Telegram, with most launch sales coming from Telegram, not the timeline.

## Related (from Full Playbooks)

**The complete minimal online business (2025-03):**
1. Find a validated product or service, replicate it, and make it better.
2. Build a landing page with bolt.new with a prominent "buy now" button; take payments through Whop.
3. Find a content style in your niche that demonstrably gets views and double down.
4. Build an email list with an automated sequence that sells for you.
5. Move content traffic to the list with a genuinely high-quality free lead magnet.
6. Send daily value emails and pitch the product once a week.

Trigger when the user asks to write or rewrite a tweet, thread, LinkedIn post, hook, title, caption, or article "for engagement/reach/virality", asks "why isn't my content performing", asks whether to make something a video or a text post, asks for help with a title or thumbnail, or shares a draft that is dense, jargon-heavy, or mechanism-first and wants it to land with a wider audience.
